turns.name: Blaise Agüera y Arcas
turns.text:
Good morning, and thank you for coming. Here's why I wanted this room together. Knowledge has never lived inside individual heads. It lives in the cultural ratchet: writing, libraries, journals, peer review, courts. These are institutions that let knowledge build up across generations without anyone needing to rebuild the whole thing. Those institutions were cracking long before generative AI, and the concept note is right about that. What's new is that the ratchet now partly runs in silicon. Large models are trained on the accumulated record of human exchange, and they're starting to take part in it.

So I don't think this is mainly a detection problem or a hype problem. It's an institution-design problem. By tomorrow afternoon I'd like us to have a manifesto short enough to read aloud, and six to ten interventions someone here will actually build. My bias is toward role templates for mixed human–AI knowledge work: reviewer, auditor, adversary, archivist. Each role should come with clear stakes, independence built in, and humans still in the loop. What makes a court different from cable news isn't a greater number of voices. It's structure.

The one thing I most want argued about: the note I co-wrote calls these systems "statistical models" and treats saying they "know" as a category error. I don't sign that sentence. I think prediction is intelligence. But I don't want this to turn into a vocabulary fight. The real question is whether our institutions should be designed as if AI is a tool we use or a participant we govern. That question decides almost everything else on the roadmap, so let's argue about it openly.

recall.query: cultural ratchet collective intelligence knowledge institutions
institutional alignment agent institutions humans remain in the loop
is AI really intelligent, deflationary statistical model, goalposts

turns.name: Geoffrey Bilder
turns.text:
Morning. I'll be brief, and I'll start by admitting I'm the one who put "statistical model" into that concept note. So Blaise and I have our argument ready-made, and it's a real one.

I convened this because I spent eighteen years building plumbing for the scholarly record: identifiers, metadata, Crossmark, similarity checking. Most of what we're now calling an "AI crisis" was already there. For decades we've used publication as a stand-in for productivity. Then we tried to catch the resulting fraud just before publication with detection tools. That was a losing, expensive fight long before large language models turned up. The dysfunction is largely self-inflicted. What machine learning changes is the cost of producing plausible junk, which drops to zero. So I want us to keep separate what was broken, what was breaking and what's now breaking faster.

What I want out of today is things we can build. I also want every piece of infrastructure we propose to come with real exit: open code, open data, full dumps, forkability. Calling something "nonprofit" or "community" guarantees nothing. And please, nobody call any of it "free." Somebody maintains it.

On Blaise's question, I'll say where I stand. I don't think these systems know anything. I think they reflect back the intentions of the people whose writing they were trained on. That isn't nitpicking, because it's the difference between treating a predictive-policing tool as intelligent and seeing it as a database of old patterns and old biases. So here's what I most want argued about: whether we govern the tool or govern the people and institutions who use it. My bet is that trust comes from context, meaning provenance, affiliations, funders and the history of corrections, and not from how fluent the output sounds. Tell me why I'm wrong.

recall.query: why the term artificial intelligence assumes the answer; statistical model
decouple career evaluation from publication; self-inflicted dysfunction
context over content trust signals provenance metadata

turns.name: David Krakauer
turns.text:
I'm an evolutionary theorist. I study intelligence, and lately I've been studying stupidity, which I've come to think is the more urgent subject. Humans have always put their thinking into tools: the tally, the abacus, the map, writing. What I want to ask of every tool is what's left in us when you take it away. A map leaves you knowing the territory. Satellite navigation leaves you lost. I call the first kind complementary and the second competitive. The tools we're building for scholarship today are opaque, they reach billions of people, and many of those people have little prior competence. My models put that in the regime that predicts competence collapse. The danger isn't only error. It's error nobody can detect anymore, because the capacities that would have caught it were handed to the machine.

Blaise, Geoffrey, I'd split your difference differently. I don't think prediction is intelligence. These systems have extraordinary capability, the way a calculator does, and capability isn't understanding. But "a mirror of old intentions" undersells them too. They're strange, mind-like artifacts. Whether we call them tools or participants matters less than whether the combined system of human and tool leaves us more intelligent or less.

So here's what I'd like us to produce. First, principles that tell apart tools that enhance cognition from tools that replace it. Second, norms about sequence: competence first, the tool after. Third, audits of what people can still do without the tool, not what they report about themselves. The one thing I most want argued about is whether keeping a human "in the loop" means anything once that human has stopped checking.

recall.query: competitive versus complementary tools competence collapse
science of stupidity undetectable error outsourced capacities
